344	    private static func defaultInputDevice() -> AudioDeviceID {
345	        var addr = address(kAudioHardwarePropertyDefaultInputDevice)
346	        var device = AudioDeviceID(0)
347	        var size = UInt32(MemoryLayout<AudioDeviceID>.size)
348	        guard AudioObjectGetPropertyData(AudioObjectID(kAudioObjectSystemObject),
349	                                         &addr, 0, nil, &size, &device) == noErr else {
350	            return AudioDeviceID(kAudioObjectUnknown)

353	    }

355	    private static func fourCC(_ value: UInt32) -> String {
356	        let bytes = [UInt8((value >> 24) & 0xFF), UInt8((value >> 16) & 0xFF),
357	                     UInt8((value >> 8) & 0xFF), UInt8(value & 0xFF)]
358	        return (String(bytes: bytes, encoding: .macOSRoman) ?? "????")
359	            .trimmingCharacters(in: .whitespaces)
360	    }

362	    /// Every device that exposes input channels, as CoreAudio sees it now.
363	    static func inputDevices() -> [InputDevice] {
364	        var addr = address(kAudioHardwarePropertyDevices)
365	        var size: UInt32 = 0
366	        let system = AudioObjectID(kAudioObjectSystemObject)
367	        guard AudioObjectGetPropertyDataSize(system, &addr, 0, nil, &size) == noErr,
368	              size > 0 else { return [] }
369	        var ids = [AudioDeviceID](repeating: 0,
370	                                  count: Int(size) / MemoryLayout<AudioDeviceID>.size)
371	        guard AudioObjectGetPropertyData(system, &addr, 0, nil, &size, &ids) == noErr else {
372	            return []
373	        }
374	        let defaultDevice = defaultInputDevice()
375	        return ids.compactMap { id in
376	            let channels = inputChannels(id)
377	            guard channels > 0 else { return nil }
378	            return InputDevice(
379	                name: string(id, kAudioObjectPropertyName) ?? "(unnamed)",
380	                uid: string(id, kAudioDevicePropertyDeviceUID) ?? "(no uid)",
381	                transport: uint32(id, kAudioDevicePropertyTransportType).map(fourCC) ?? "????",
382	                sampleRate: float64(id, kAudioDevicePropertyNominalSampleRate) ?? 0,
383	                channels: channels,
384	                isAlive: (uint32(id, kAudioDevicePropertyDeviceIsAlive) ?? 0) != 0,

388	                isRunningSomewhere:

394	    /// Everything about the input device set *except* whether IO is running on
395	    /// it — i.e. the part that changing means the hardware changed under us,
396	    /// rather than us having started or stopped capturing.
397	    private static func identities(_ devices: [InputDevice]) -> [String] {
398	        devices.map {
399	            "\($0.uid)|\($0.name)|\($0.transport)|\($0.sampleRate)|\($0.channels)"
400	                + "|\($0.isAlive)|\($0.isDefault)"
401	        }
402	    }

404	    private static func describe(_ devices: [InputDevice]) -> String {
405	        guard !devices.isEmpty else { return "inputs=NONE" }
406	        let rendered = devices.map { device in
407	            "\(device.isDefault ? "*" : "")\"\(device.name)\"/\(device.transport)"
408	                + "/\(Int(device.sampleRate))Hz/\(device.channels)ch"
409	                + "/alive=\(device.isAlive ? "y" : "n")"
410	                + "/running=\(device.isRunningSomewhere ? "y" : "n")"
411	        }
412	        return "inputs=[\(rendered.joined(separator: " "))]"
413	    }

3	/// A tiny **operational** log — separate from `laughs.jsonl` — so that "the
4	/// service stopped" is self-diagnosing instead of invisible. It records lifecycle
5	/// events (started / stopped / slept / woke / reconfigured) and errors, one line
6	/// per event as `ISO8601␠␠LEVEL␠␠message`, to
7	/// `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughcounter.log`.
8	///
9	/// Writes are serialised on a private queue and the file is rotated once when it
10	/// passes ~1 MB, so it can never grow without bound. Everything is also mirrored
11	/// to `NSLog` so it still shows up in Console.app.
12	final class AppLog {
13	    static let shared = AppLog()
14	
15	    let fileURL: URL
16	    private let queue = DispatchQueue(label: "com.laughcounter.applog")
17	    private let maxBytes: UInt64 = 1_000_000
18	    private let iso: ISO8601DateFormatter = {
19	        let f = ISO8601DateFormatter()
20	        f.formatOptions = [.withInternetDateTime]
21	        return f
22	    }()
23	
24	    private init() {
25	        let base = FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory,
26	                                            in: .userDomainMask)[0]
27	        let dir = base.appendingPathComponent("LaughCounter", isDirectory: true)
28	        try? FileManager.default.createDirectory(at: dir, withIntermediateDirectories: true)
29	        fileURL = dir.appendingPathComponent("laughcounter.log")
30	    }
31	
32	    func log(_ message: String, level: String = "INFO") {
33	        NSLog("LaughCounter: %@", message)
34	        let stamp = iso.string(from: Date())
35	        queue.async { [weak self] in
36	            guard let self = self,
37	                  let data = "\(stamp)  \(level)  \(message)\n".data(using: .utf8) else { return }
38	            self.rotateIfNeeded()
39	            if let handle = try? FileHandle(forWritingTo: self.fileURL) {
40	                defer { try? handle.close() }
41	                handle.seekToEndOfFile()
42	                handle.write(data)
43	            } else {
44	                try? data.write(to: self.fileURL)
45	            }
46	        }
47	    }
48	
49	    /// Rotate `laughcounter.log` → `laughcounter.1.log` once it passes `maxBytes`,
50	    /// keeping exactly one previous file. Called on the write queue.
51	    private func rotateIfNeeded() {
52	        guard let attrs = try? FileManager.default.attributesOfItem(atPath: fileURL.path),
53	              let size = attrs[.size] as? UInt64, size > maxBytes else { return }
54	        let rotated = fileURL.deletingPathExtension().appendingPathExtension("1.log")
55	        try? FileManager.default.removeItem(at: rotated)
56	        try? FileManager.default.moveItem(at: fileURL, to: rotated)
57	    }
58	}

Yes — and please **don't quit the app, replug the mic, or restart anything yet**. This is the exact state `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` says we've never captured live: the app's own diagnostics (shipped in #79) are sampling the CoreAudio HAL every 5s right now, and the verdict line only exists while the failure is present.

**Run this — one block, copy-paste, nothing to install:**

```bash
L="$HOME/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/laughcounter.log"
O="$HOME/Desktop/lc-diag.txt"
{
  echo "=== now: $(date -u +%FT%TZ) ==="
  ps -o pid,etime,command -p "$(pgrep -f LaughCounter.app | head -1)"
  echo "=== recent sleep/wake ==="
  pmset -g log | grep -iE " Sleep  | Wake  |DarkWake" | tail -20
  echo "=== last 250 log lines ==="
  tail -n 250 "$L"
  echo "=== every stall/device event this run ==="
  grep -nE "AUDIO STALL|audio recovered|input devices|no signal|audio health|audio snapshot" "$L" | tail -60
} > "$O" 2>&1; echo "wrote $O"
```

Then paste `~/Desktop/lc-diag.txt` here (or the tail of it).

**Two things only you can see, which the log can't tell me:**

1. **The menu bar icon.** 🔇 = the app knows audio stopped arriving; 😄 = it believes it's healthy and capturing; 🎙️ = it isn't listening at all (paused / no mic access). Which one is it?
2. **Is the mic dead system-wide?** System Settings → Sound → Input, speak, watch the level meter. Moving = only our app is broken. Flat = the device is wedged for everyone, which is the failure mode where the fix is on our teardown path.

**What the answer decides** (this is the open question #79 left unresolved, so the log line picks the theory rather than me guessing):

| Log line | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `AUDIO STALL … running=y` | The running stream is *ours* and it's dead → our restart churn wedged it. Fix goes in the restart path. |
| `AUDIO STALL … running=n`, device present, nonzero rate | Device is fine, our engine never got buffers → start/reconcile path. |
| `inputs=NONE`, or `alive=n`, or `0Hz` | The mic is gone from the HAL — hardware/enumeration, and the system-wide meter test above confirms it. |
| No `AUDIO STALL` at all | The app stopped listening on purpose (an `offReason`) — a different bug, in the wake-resume path. |

Once you've captured the file, feel free to replug/restart to get yourself working again — the evidence is already on disk, and the log rotates only at 1 MB so it won't be lost.

> ⚠️ Waiting on you: `lc-diag.txt`, the menu bar icon, and the System Settings input meter. I haven't changed any code — per the repo's own lifecycle doc, this bug doesn't get a fix written until the live diagnostic says which theory is right, and a wrong guess here rapid-cycles the mic, which is the thing that wedges it.

Comment class: correction — same defect thread; the diagnostic came back and it changes the diagnosis.

## The verdict: this is not the wedge, and it's not a stall

The log rules out both theories `mac-audio-lifecycle.md` was waiting to decide between. Buffers are arriving **at full rate** — 3545 per 600s = 5.908/s against the theoretical 5.859 — so `AUDIO STALL` never fires and never should have. The device is `alive=y`, `running=y`, 48000Hz/2ch, and the tap format agrees.

Every sample is **exactly zero**, for 31 minutes and counting:

```
05:02:28  audio health: listening buffers=38110 … peak=0.0000
05:02:28  ERROR  no signal: 230 buffers … every sample was zero
05:12:33  ERROR  no signal: 3545 buffers … every sample was zero
05:22:38  ERROR  no signal: 3545 buffers … every sample was zero
05:32:43  ERROR  no signal: 3545 buffers … every sample was zero
```

That's the **third failure mode** `AudioDiagnostics` anticipated in its comments and had never observed: the stream is alive and carrying digital silence. A real mic always has a noise floor; exact zero across half an hour is not a quiet room. With System Settings also showing a dead meter, the BRIO came back from display sleep **enumerated but not actually capturing** — system-wide, not just for us.

The timeline that matters, and it's a suspect:

```
05:01:18  could not start listening: … inputs=NONE      ← 3h40m of this
05:01:45  displays woke while listening was down
05:01:48  WARN  input devices changed — "Logitech BRIO"/usb/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y
05:01:48  listening started (sampleRate=48000, channels=2)   ← same second
```

The BRIO reappeared and we opened it **within the same second**, with no settle window at all. The doc already knows this shape ("the mic can still be re-enumerating when the settle window closes") — here we didn't wait even once. Grabbing a half-enumerated USB device is a plausible way to end up pinned to a stream that never carries audio.

## Confirmed app defect, independent of cause

Your screenshot shows **😄 0 📺 0** — the app is reporting healthy listening while it has logged `no signal` at ERROR four times in a row. `isStalled` only trips on *absent* buffers, so `statusText`, the icon and the tooltip all sail straight past a stream of pure zeros. That is precisely the sin #79 was written to eliminate — "the one symptom the owner sees, saying the one thing that isn't true" — recurring one layer up. It also takes up to 600s to notice, and nothing ever attempts recovery. I'll fix that regardless of what causes the zeros.

## One test, 30 seconds, and it decides the rest

**Quit LaughCounter** (menu → Quit, so teardown runs), then re-check System Settings → Sound → Input:

- **Meter comes alive with the app dead** → *we* pinned the device in the bad state by grabbing it mid-enumeration. Cause is app-side, and the fix is a settle window plus a no-signal recovery cycle.
- **Meter still dead** → the BRIO/coreaudiod is broken on its own and no app-side change can capture audio. The fix is then bounded to honest status, faster detection, and a bounded recovery attempt.

To get yourself working again afterwards, in order — but only **after** that check, since each step destroys the evidence:

```bash
sudo killall coreaudiod     # restarts CoreAudio; usually enough, no replug needed
```
and if that doesn't do it, unplug/replug the BRIO.

> ⚠️ Waiting on you: the input meter reading **with LaughCounter quit**. That one bit picks between "our premature grab caused it" and "the device died on its own", which is the difference between a recovery fix and a reporting fix. I've written no code yet — but the dishonest 😄 is confirmed and I'll fix it either way, so tell me the meter result and I'll implement on `claude/sound-input-sleep-issue-9eh40k`.

284	                // still re-enumerating when the settle window ends and there is

287	                // again, doubling each time (2s, 4s … 32s) and giving up after

296	    /// Back-off retry after a failed start, generation-guarded like every other
297	    /// deferred restart: an intentional stop, or any restart accepted meanwhile,
298	    /// moves the generation and this retry aborts rather than re-acquiring the mic
299	    /// behind it. Main-thread only.
300	    private func scheduleStartRetry(generation: Int) {
301	        let attempt = startFailureStreak
302	        // Double up to the ceiling, then keep checking at that interval for as
303	        // long as the counter is meant to be on. Deliberately never gives up: the
304	        // measured cause of a long outage is the input device being torn down
305	        // while the displays sleep, which lasted 28 minutes in one observation —
306	        // no bounded ladder covers that, and the old five attempts (~62s) expired
307	        // with the cause still fully present, telling the user to reconnect a
308	        // microphone that was fine. A start attempt is now a cheap format read
309	        // that throws before touching the tap, and one a minute is far below any
310	        // rate that could cycle a USB mic. (#76)
311	        let delay = min(Double(1 << min(attempt, 6)), maxBackoffDelay)
312	        if attempt <= maxStartRetries {
313	            AppLog.shared.log("start failed — retrying in \(Int(delay))s "
314	                + "(attempt \(attempt) of \(maxStartRetries))", level: "WARN")
315	        } else if attempt == maxStartRetries + 1 {
316	            // Announce the switch to slow checking once, then stay quiet until it
317	            // works — a line a minute for half an hour buries everything else.
318	            AppLog.shared.log("input device still unavailable — checking every "
319	                + "\(Int(maxBackoffDelay))s until it returns (expected while the "
320	                + "displays are asleep; no action needed)", level: "WARN")
321	        }
322	        DispatchQueue.main.asyncAfter(deadline: .now() + delay) { [weak self] in
323	            guard let self = self, generation == self.restartGeneration else { return }
324	            guard self.listeningIntent, !self.listening else { return }

423	    /// not listening when it went down comes back not listening.
424	    private func systemDidReturn(reason: String) {
425	        // These signals also fire with no sleep involved at all: the display
426	        // waking from the screensaver, a user switching back. Only a machine that
427	        // actually owes a resume reacts — restarting capture on every display wake

429	        guard sleeping || (listeningIntent && !listening) else { return }
430	        if pendingResumeID != nil { return }   // the burst is one return, one resume
431	        // How long we were down, measured from willSleep. Nil means we never slept:
432	        // the signal is then a backstop over a start that failed earlier, and it
433	        // buys exactly one more attempt — not a fresh retry ladder.
434	        let asleep = sleepStartedAt.map { Date().timeIntervalSince($0) }
435	        // After a long standby the USB bus was powered down and devices come back
436	        // well after the wake notification, so settle for longer before re-acquiring.

438	        let settle = standby ? standbySettleDelay : wakeSettleDelay
439	        let what = listeningIntent ? "resuming listening shortly"
440	                                   : "counter is \(offReason ?? "off"), staying off"

443	                                     standby ? "standby" : "sleep", what))

446	        }
447	        resumeID &+= 1
448	        let id = resumeID

451	        // re-enumeration can't trigger an early, un-settled restart; this resume is

456	        let generation = restartGeneration

472	            // at the moment we decide to re-acquire, which is the state that
473	            // decides whether the start about to run can possibly succeed.
474	            AppLog.shared.log("settled after \(reason) — \(self.diagnostics.snapshotLine())")

476	            // signal (no sleep behind it) gets the single attempt below instead.
477	            if asleep != nil { self.startFailureStreak = 0 }
478	            self.requestListening()

1	import AVFoundation
2	import CoreAudio
3	import Foundation
4	
5	/// Continuous health monitoring for the capture path, so a mic failure records
6	/// itself as it happens instead of being reconstructed afterwards.
7	///
8	/// Every previous round of "the mic is dead after sleep" was diagnosed from
9	/// whatever survived — and the app's own log only ever said `listening started`,
10	/// because that is all it knew. `listening` means `engine.start()` returned; it
11	/// has never meant that audio is arriving. So the app could hold a dead device
12	/// for hours and report itself healthy, which is exactly what it did.
13	///
14	/// This closes that gap with two cheap, continuous measurements:
15	///
16	/// - **Buffer liveness.** The tap reports every buffer here; a timer notices
17	///   when they stop while we believe we are capturing, and says so once
18	///   (`AUDIO STALL`), then says so again when they come back. That is the
19	///   difference between "listening" and "holding a dead device".
20	/// - **The device, from CoreAudio's own point of view.** Read straight from the
21	///   HAL, which is a property query — it does **not** open the device, so
22	///   sampling it costs nothing and cannot contribute to the rapid-cycling that
23	///   wedges a USB mic. `IsRunningSomewhere` is the one that matters: it is true
24	///   when *any* process has IO running on the device, so "no buffers arriving
25	///   while IsRunningSomewhere is true" says the stream is ours and it is dead,
26	///   rather than the device having simply gone away.

## The wedge recurred, and it lives *below* coreaudiod (#88)

It came back on 0.4.1, and in a third shape — **no `AUDIO STALL`, ever**. Buffers
were arriving at the full rate (3545 per 600s against a theoretical 3515) from a
device reporting `alive=y/running=y/48000Hz/2ch`, and **every sample was exactly
zero**, for half an hour, system-wide — System Settings → Sound → Input showed a
dead meter too. Not the stall (buffers stopped), not the vanish (`inputs=NONE`):
the mode `AudioDiagnostics` had anticipated in a comment and never seen — a
device that is enumerated and streaming and *not capturing*.

**The escalation ladder, tried in order, is the finding:**

| Attempted | Cleared it |
| --- | --- |
| Quitting LaughCounter (full `applicationWillTerminate` teardown) | no |
| `sudo killall coreaudiod` | no |
| Physically unplugging and re-plugging the mic | **yes** |

That settles what the release-the-mic invariant never could: **this wedge is not
in our process, and not in coreaudiod's user-space state either.** It survives
every client dying *and* the audio daemon being restarted from scratch; only a USB
re-enumeration takes the device out of it. Two consequences outrank the rest of
this file:

- **No in-process recovery can work, so do not build one.** A restart ladder
  against this state is pure churn — it cannot succeed, and cycling is the thing
  we already believe is dangerous. The app's whole job here is to *notice fast,
  say so honestly, and name the one remedy that works.*
- **"Release the mic on every path" is necessary but not sufficient.** The
  teardown ran correctly on Quit and the device stayed wedged. A clean exit
  prevents the IOProc-abandonment cause; it does not prevent this one.

**What shipped is reporting, not recovery.** `no signal` was already detected and
logged at ERROR every ten minutes — and it drove **nothing**: `isStalled` tripped
only on *absent* buffers, so the menu bar showed 😄 "listening" for the whole
outage while the log said the opposite. That is exactly the sin #79 set out to
kill, recurring one layer up, and it is why this round *again* had to be
reconstructed from a log instead of noticed. So `AudioDiagnostics` publishes a
three-state `health` (`ok` / `stalled` / `noSignal`), every user-facing surface
renders it, and the no-signal text says **unplug it** rather than "try Restart
listening" — because restarting is measured not to work. When a state has exactly
one remedy, the UI must name that remedy, not the generic one.

**Detection moved off the heartbeat.** The old check ran inside the 600s heartbeat
block, so a dead stream was invisible for up to ten minutes and then repeated an
identical ERROR every ten minutes for as long as it lasted. It is judged on the 5s
sample tick over a 60s window of all-zero buffers now, and logged once per
transition. 60s is safe against a quiet room by a wide margin — a real capsule
always has a noise floor, and the window covers ~350 buffers.

**The one thing this did not settle.** The device reappeared at 05:01:48 and we
opened it *in the same second*: the config-change handler and `listening started`
carry the same timestamp, after 3h40m of once-a-minute failed starts against
`inputs=NONE`. Grabbing a USB audio device mid-enumeration is a plausible way to
pin it non-capturing, and it is the only app-side action in the window — but the
mic may equally have come back broken on its own. If it recurs, measure whether a
settle delay between "device appeared" and "open it" changes the outcome. **Do not
add the delay and call it fixed**: a fix that isn't the cause looks like it worked
for exactly as long as the next episode takes to arrive.

## Diagnostics must not assume a toolchain on the owner's Mac

input.body:
Closes the evidence gap in #88, and fixes what that evidence exposed.

## What was measured

The wedge recurred on 0.4.1 and was captured live for the first time. It arrived in a shape **neither open theory predicted — there was no `AUDIO STALL` at all.** Buffers were arriving at the full rate (3545 per 600s against a theoretical 3515) from a device reporting `alive=y/running=y/48000Hz/2ch`, with **every sample exactly zero**, for half an hour, system-wide (System Settings showed a dead input meter too).

```
05:01:48  input devices changed — *"Logitech BRIO"/usb/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y/running=n
05:01:48  listening started (sampleRate=48000, channels=2)     ← same second
05:02:28  audio health: listening buffers=38110 … peak=0.0000
05:12:33  ERROR  no signal: 3545 buffers … every sample was zero
05:22:38  ERROR  no signal: 3545 buffers … every sample was zero
05:32:43  ERROR  no signal: 3545 buffers … every sample was zero
```

The escalation ladder, tried in order, is the finding:

| Attempted | Cleared it |
| --- | --- |
| Quitting LaughCounter (full `applicationWillTerminate` teardown) | no |
| `sudo killall coreaudiod` | no |
| Physically unplugging and re-plugging the mic | **yes** |

**This wedge lives below coreaudiod** — it survives every client dying *and* the audio daemon restarting from scratch; only a USB re-enumeration clears it. So no in-process recovery can work, and a restart ladder against it would be pure churn against a state it cannot fix. "Release the mic on every path" turns out to be necessary but not sufficient: the teardown ran correctly and the device stayed wedged.

## What this changes

The fix is **reporting, not recovery**. `no signal` was already detected and logged at ERROR every ten minutes — and it drove **nothing**. `isStalled` tripped only on *absent* buffers, so the menu bar showed 😄 "listening" for the entire outage while the log said the opposite. That is the sin #79 set out to kill, recurring one layer up, and it is why this round *again* had to be reconstructed from a log instead of noticed.

- `AudioDiagnostics` publishes a three-state `health` (`ok` / `stalled` / `noSignal`) in place of the `isStalled` bool, with a single `setHealth()` that logs the transition and notifies — so the log and the menu bar cannot disagree.
- No-signal is judged on the **5s sample tick over a 60s run** of all-zero buffers, not inside the 600s heartbeat block: caught in a minute rather than ten, and logged once per transition instead of repeating an identical ERROR every ten minutes for as long as it lasts. 60s of exact zeros cannot be a quiet room — a real capsule always has a noise floor and the window covers ~350 buffers.
- The icon (⚠️), status line, tooltip and menu tooltip all render the new state, and the no-signal text names the **only** remedy measured to work: unplug and reconnect. It deliberately does *not* offer "Restart listening", now known not to help.

Stall thresholds and behaviour are unchanged.

## Verification

`swift build` cannot run in a Linux session, and per `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` **compile-green is not a gate for this file anyway** — two crash-on-launch builds have shipped past CI before. The feature-branch DMG workflow builds it on macOS; it is not verified until it has actually started on a Mac and the menu bar has been seen to show ⚠️ in the failing state.

Reachability note: the new state is only reachable with a mic that is streaming silence, so the cheap live check is that a **healthy** launch still shows 😄 and the log still reads `audio health: listening … peak=<nonzero>`.

## Docs

`dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` records the escalation ladder, marks the now-superseded "don't write the fix until an `AUDIO STALL` line with `running=y`" instruction so a future session doesn't chase a signal that never comes, and keeps the one unsettled suspect: **we opened the device in the same second it reappeared**, after 3h40m of once-a-minute failed starts. That may have pinned it mid-enumeration, or the mic may have come back broken on its own — the doc says to measure a settle delay if it recurs, and explicitly not to add one and call it fixed.

content.text:
No. Not if "work" means your mic survives the next sleep — it almost certainly won't.

Let me be precise about what I actually shipped:

| | Fixed? |
|---|---|
| Mic dies after sleep | **No.** Nothing I changed touches the cause. |
| Mic recovers on its own once dead | **No** — and your ladder proves nothing in software can do it. Only the replug. |
| App tells you it's dead | **Yes**, within ~60s instead of never. |

So it's a fix to the *reporting*, not the failure. You'll still lose the mic; you'll just find out in a minute instead of discovering it hours later. That's worth having — this bug has now been reconstructed after the fact three times because the menu bar said 😄 — but it is not what you asked for, and I shouldn't let the PR's length imply otherwise.

Two further honesty items:

**The reporting fix itself is unverified.** It's uncompiled (no Swift toolchain here), and the ⚠️ path is only reachable when a mic is actually streaming silence — so it can't be exercised until this recurs. Mechanically it's straightforward, but I haven't seen it run.

**I weakened my own suspect while writing this up.** I flagged the same-second grab as the candidate cause. But look at what the HAL reported at that instant:

```
05:01:48  *"Logitech BRIO"/usb/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y/running=n
```

Real name, sane rate, sane channel count. The doc's own signature for a mid-enumeration device is `"(unnamed)"/????/0Hz`. So by every property the app can read, the BRIO looked *fully settled* when we opened it. That's evidence against "we grabbed it too early" — it doesn't kill the theory (HAL properties being readable doesn't mean the USB streaming interface is ready), but it's weaker than I implied.

## What I'd do next, and why I didn't just do it

There are two directions, and they're different in kind:

1. **A settle delay before opening a just-appeared device.** Cheap, low-risk, plausible. But it's a guess against a cause I just argued is shakier than I thought — and per the doc, a fix that isn't the cause looks like it worked for exactly as long as the next episode takes to arrive. That's how this bug has survived several rounds already.

2. **Make the failure impossible to sit through.** Independent of root cause: on `noSignal`, fire a user notification and a chime rather than only changing an emoji you have to be looking at. You lost an evening because the failure was silent, not because it was mysterious. This one I'm confident about — it doesn't depend on any theory being right.

I'd take **2** now and hold **1** until the next episode gives us something to test it against. But if you'd rather have the settle delay in the same build and accept it's speculative, say so — it's a small change and you're the one living with the outage.

> ⚠️ Direct answer: **no, the mic will very likely die again.** PR #100 makes that visible in ~60s instead of invisible; it does not prevent or recover it. Tell me which of 1 / 2 / both you want and I'll add it to the same PR.

13	/// quiet, and a quiet config-change observer means the app stops noticing that
14	/// its microphone disappeared.
15	final class AudioHub {
16	    private var engine: AVAudioEngine
17	    private var configObserver: NSObjectProtocol?
18	
19	    /// Called for every captured buffer, on the audio thread.
20	    var onBuffer: ((AVAudioPCMBuffer, AVAudioTime) -> Void)?
21	
22	    /// Called on the main queue when CoreAudio reports that the current engine's
23	    /// configuration changed (device added, removed, or switched under us).
24	    var onConfigurationChange: (() -> Void)?
25	
26	    /// The input format currently in use (valid only once `start(format:)` ran).
27	    private(set) var activeFormat: AVAudioFormat?
28	
29	    var isRunning: Bool { engine.isRunning }
30	
31	    init() {
32	        engine = Self.makeEngine()
33	        observeConfigurationChange()
34	    }
35	
36	    /// Build an engine that is safe to `prepare()`.
37	    ///
38	    /// `AVAudioEngine` initializes its graph inside `prepare()` and asserts that
39	    /// at least one node is attached — `inputNode != nullptr || outputNode !=
40	    /// nullptr` — raising an uncatchable NSException when none is. A freshly
41	    /// constructed engine has none: `inputNode` is created lazily *on first
42	    /// access*, and touching the property is what attaches it. So materialize it
43	    /// here, as part of building an engine, rather than leaving it to a call
44	    /// order somewhere else.
45	    ///
46	    /// The pre-rebuild code survived only by accident: `requestListening()` calls
47	    /// `stop()`, which reaches `engine.inputNode.removeTap(onBus: 0)` and
48	    /// materialized the node on the single long-lived engine long before any
49	    /// `prepare()`. Rebuilding the engine after that call removed the accident,
50	    /// and every launch crashed one second in. (#72)
51	    private static func makeEngine() -> AVAudioEngine {
52	        let engine = AVAudioEngine()
53	        _ = engine.inputNode   // attaches it; do not "simplify" this away
54	        return engine
55	    }
56	
57	    deinit {
58	        if let observer = configObserver {
59	            NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver(observer)
60	        }
61	    }
62	
63	    /// Build a fresh engine and return its validated live input format, **without**
64	    /// starting capture. The input node's format is only reliable after prepare;
65	    /// returning it first lets the detector be configured to match *before* any
66	    /// audio flows (the analyzer must exist before buffers arrive, or the first
67	    /// buffers are dropped and analysis can fail to start).
68	    ///
69	    /// The engine is replaced here rather than reused, and that is the fix for
70	    /// #61. An `AVAudioEngine` caches the input hardware format when its input
71	    /// node is first materialized, and the cache does not follow the device: after
72	    /// CoreAudio tears the input down — a USB mic re-enumerating, or coreaudiod
73	    /// dropping its contexts when the display sleeps — `inputNode.outputFormat(
74	    /// forBus: 0)` keeps reporting the *old* rate. `installTap` validates against
75	    /// the freshly-queried hardware format instead, the two disagree, and it
76	    /// raises an uncatchable NSException. That killed the app on every single
77	    /// configuration change (six for six over fifteen days) — not the rare race
78	    /// the previous guard assumed, because comparing the stale cache against
79	    /// itself always passed. A new engine reads the hardware fresh, so the guard
80	    /// in `start(format:)` is meaningful again and the two formats agree.
81	    func prepareFormat() throws -> AVAudioFormat {
82	        renewEngine()
83	        // Trapped as well as installTap: #59 wrapped only the tap install, and
84	        // prepare() then raised from a path with no trap in it at all. Anything
85	        // that can raise on the way to capture gets the same treatment. (#72)
86	        try ObjCExceptionTrap.run { engine.prepare() }
87	        return try validatedFormat()
88	    }
89	
90	    /// The tap format, checked against the *hardware* format that `installTap`
91	    /// asserts on.
92	    ///
93	    /// Read `inputFormat(forBus: 0)`, not `outputFormat`: `outputFormat` is the
94	    /// bus's output format, and with the input device torn down it still reports
95	    /// a plausible 48 kHz while `inputFormat` correctly reports 0. Checking
96	    /// `outputFormat` therefore could not detect an absent microphone at all — it
97	    /// waved through starts that could never succeed and left `installTap` to
98	    /// raise, which is what the exception trap kept catching once a minute while
99	    /// the displays slept. Requiring the two to agree means `installTap` is never
100	    /// reached in the mismatch state. (#76)
101	    private func validatedFormat() throws -> AVAudioFormat {
102	        let input = engine.inputNode
103	        let hardware = input.inputFormat(forBus: 0)
104	        let bus = input.outputFormat(forBus: 0)
105	        guard hardware.sampleRate > 0, hardware.channelCount > 0 else {
106	            throw NSError(domain: "LaughCounter", code: 1, userInfo: [
107	                NSLocalizedDescriptionKey:
108	                    "no input hardware — the microphone is not available "
109	                    + "(sampleRate=\(hardware.sampleRate), channels=\(hardware.channelCount))",
110	            ])
111	        }
112	        guard hardware.sampleRate == bus.sampleRate,
113	              hardware.channelCount == bus.channelCount else {
114	            throw NSError(domain: "LaughCounter", code: 2, userInfo: [
115	                NSLocalizedDescriptionKey:
116	                    "input format unsettled "
117	                    + "(hardware \(hardware.sampleRate)Hz/\(hardware.channelCount)ch, "
118	                    + "bus \(bus.sampleRate)Hz/\(bus.channelCount)ch)",
119	            ])
120	        }
121	        return bus
122	    }
123	
124	    /// Install the tap and start capture, using a format from `prepareFormat()`.
125	    func start(format: AVAudioFormat) throws {
126	        let input = engine.inputNode
127	        // Re-validate against the hardware immediately before the tap: the device
128	        // can still vanish between prepareFormat() and here (dock unplug,
129	        // wake-time re-enumeration), and a mismatch reaching installTap is what
130	        // raises. Checking the same pair as prepareFormat did, because the bus
131	        // format alone cannot tell an absent device from a present one. (#76)
132	        let live = try validatedFormat()
133	        guard live.sampleRate == format.sampleRate,
134	              live.channelCount == format.channelCount else {
135	            throw NSError(domain: "LaughCounter", code: 3, userInfo: [
136	                NSLocalizedDescriptionKey:
137	                    "input device changed between prepare and start "
138	                    + "(expected \(format.sampleRate)Hz/\(format.channelCount)ch, "
139	                    + "live \(live.sampleRate)Hz/\(live.channelCount)ch)",
140	            ])
141	        }
142	        input.removeTap(onBus: 0)   // no-op if none installed; keeps restart clean
143	        // Backstop: installTap raises an *uncatchable* NSException if its format
144	        // disagrees with the live hardware, and Swift cannot catch one — it aborts
145	        // the process, skipping the tap teardown in applicationWillTerminate and
146	        // leaving the IOProc registered, which is exactly what wedges a USB webcam
147	        // mic until it is physically re-plugged. This is not theoretical and not
148	        // dead code: it demonstrably caught that exception once a minute while the
149	        // displays slept, which is the only reason the app survived. The guard
150	        // above should now keep us off that path; this stays because there is no
151	        // atomic API and being wrong here costs the microphone.
152	        try ObjCExceptionTrap.run {
153	            input.installTap(onBus: 0, bufferSize: 8192, format: format) { [weak self] buffer, when in
154	                self?.onBuffer?(buffer, when)
155	            }
156	        }
157	        try engine.start()
158	        activeFormat = format
159	    }
160	
161	    func stop() {
162	        engine.inputNode.removeTap(onBus: 0)
163	        // Unconditional: engine.stop() is safe on a non-running engine, and it also
164	        // releases what engine.prepare() allocated — a prepare()-then-throw path
165	        // (prepareFormat/configure failing before start) would otherwise leave the
166	        // initialized input unit holding the device.
167	        engine.stop()
168	        activeFormat = nil
169	    }
170	
171	    /// Tear the current engine down and put a fresh one in its place. Stopping
172	    /// first is what keeps the release-the-mic invariant: dropping the last
173	    /// reference to a *running* engine would abandon its tap and IOProc on the
174	    /// device instead of deregistering them.
175	    private func renewEngine() {
176	        stop()
177	        engine = Self.makeEngine()
178	        observeConfigurationChange()
179	    }
180	
181	    /// (Re)point the configuration-change observation at the current engine.
182	    private func observeConfigurationChange() {
183	        if let observer = configObserver {
184	            NotificationCenter.default.removeObserver(observer)
185	        }

189	            forName: .AVAudioEngineConfigurationChange, object: engine, queue: .main

Based on the search results, I found relevant information about AVAudioEngine, inputNode, and USB microphone issues on macOS:

## Key Findings

**Related Issues with AVAudioEngine and Input Nodes:**

AVAudioEngine doesn't give developers an opportunity to state their intentions explicitly on macOS, and there is no API that lets you specify that you are building an output-only engine and don't require input abilities.

**Rebuilding and Configuration Issues:**

When switching between configurations with external microphones formatted at different sample rates, developers stop AVAudioEngine and detach nodes, update the shared audio session, and reconstruct the audio graph by attaching nodes and reconnecting them, and then restart the engine. There is a reported race-condition between switching settings and rebuilding the audio graph.

**Device Switching Problems:**

When switching audio input sources, stopping and starting the engine on a route change does not help, neither does calling reset(), and disconnecting and reconnecting the input node does not help either. The only thing that reliably helps is discarding the whole engine and creating a new one.

**macOS Specific Challenges:**

On macOS, you're as likely to be interacting with cheap USB podcasting microphones as professional studio interfaces, and if you require users to override device selection and buffer sizes, you might encounter trouble and painful workarounds.

The search results suggest that repeatedly rebuilding AVAudioEngine configurations with USB microphones can lead to state management issues that may cause the system to hang or stop working properly.

AVAudioEngine creates a hidden aggregate device (CADefaultDeviceAggregate-*) at init time, and when the system default output changes, this aggregate can become stale. The engine reports isRunning == true and buffers report completion, but no audio reaches the speakers.

This appears to be a known problem in CoreAudio where AVAudioEngine's hidden aggregate device goes stale when the system default audio output changes (Bluetooth connect/disconnect, HDMI, speaker switch). Only manually switching the output device and back fixes it.

Additionally, AVAudioEngineConfigurationChangeNotification sometimes doesn't fire for background/accessory apps, which can prevent automatic detection of these device state changes.

The most detailed discussion of this issue appears to be in a GitHub issue (index 1) from March 2026, which specifically addresses strategies for recovering from stale aggregate devices using CoreAudio HAL listeners and periodic health checks.

content.content:
# AVAudioEngine Stale Aggregate Device Failure Mode

## Symptoms
The engine reports `isRunning == true` and audio buffers complete successfully, yet no sound reaches the speakers. Manual switching of the output device and back restores functionality.

## Root Cause
AVAudioEngine creates a hidden aggregate device (`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-*`) during initialization. When system default audio output changes—such as Bluetooth connection/disconnection or HDMI switching—this aggregate becomes stale. The `AVAudioEngineConfigurationChangeNotification` may fail to trigger for background or accessory applications, leaving the engine unaware of the device change.

## Trigger Events
- Bluetooth speaker connection or disconnection
- HDMI device changes
- Speaker output switching
- System default audio output modifications

## Proposed Recovery Strategy

A three-layer approach is recommended:

# AVAudioEngine Stale Aggregate Device Failure Mode

## Symptoms
The engine reports `isRunning == true` and audio buffers complete successfully, yet no sound reaches the speakers. Manual switching of the output device and back restores functionality.

## Root Cause
AVAudioEngine creates a hidden aggregate device (`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-*`) during initialization. When system default audio output changes—such as Bluetooth connection/disconnection or HDMI switching—this aggregate becomes stale. The `AVAudioEngineConfigurationChangeNotification` may fail to trigger for background or accessory applications, leaving the engine unaware of the device change.

## Trigger Events
- Bluetooth speaker connection or disconnection
- HDMI device changes
- Speaker output switching
- System default audio output modifications

## Proposed Recovery Strategy

A three-layer approach is recommended:

1. **CoreAudio HAL listener** monitoring `kAudioHardwarePropertyDefaultOutputDevice` for reliable detection
2. **AVAudioEngineConfigurationChangeNotification** as a backup for sample rate changes
3. **Periodic health check** (30-second intervals) comparing engine device ID against system default, triggering rebuild if mismatched

Recovery involves stopping the engine, detaching nodes, resetting, re-attaching nodes, preparing, and restarting with a 100-200ms debounce to prevent format mismatch errors.

That research changes the picture, and you're right that I was wrong to stop where I did. Three findings:

**1. The symptom shape is a known CoreAudio failure, not exotic.** `AVAudioEngine` creates a hidden per-client aggregate device (`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-*`) **at init time**, and it can go stale: engine reports running, buffers complete, no audio flows. Exactly our shape. ([cc-skills#73](https://github.com/terrylica/cc-skills/issues/73))

**2. Which means our retry ladder is doing something no ordinary app does.** Reading `AudioHub` rather than the doc summary: `prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` → `makeEngine()`, and `makeEngine()` touches `engine.inputNode` — *that* is what opens the default input and mints the hidden aggregate. So every retry attempt creates and destroys an aggregate device inside coreaudiod. Your log shows **~210 of them** across the 3h40m outage, one a minute.

**3. We already have the answer for free and don't use it.** `AudioDiagnostics.inputDevices()` reads the HAL via `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` every 5 seconds — pure property queries, no device open. The ladder ignores it and builds an entire audio engine to ask the same question. The lifecycle doc even says this outright and it was never acted on:

> the "cheap format read" the retry-ladder comment in `AppDelegate` claims is actually a full device open/close, once a minute for as long as the mic is missing

And the same-second grab wasn't the ladder — it was `audioConfigChanged()` firing on device arrival and opening it immediately. Both paths funnel through `finishListening()`.

So: gate the only place that opens the device on the free probe we're already running.

**"Only a replug clears it" is not "we didn't cause it."** Those are separate
claims and this file conflated them for one round: the ladder above establishes
that the state is *irreversible once triggered*, and says nothing about what
triggers it. The trigger question is answered below.

## Never build an `AVAudioEngine` to ask whether a microphone exists (#88)

This is the thing that made LaughCounter abnormal, and no other app on the owner's
Mac wedges the mic on sleep.

`AudioHub.prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` → `makeEngine()`, and `makeEngine()`
touches `engine.inputNode`. **That property access opens the default input device
and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod**
(`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`); a failed start tears it back down. So a
"retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus an aggregate
create/destroy. One measured outage ran that cycle **~210 times over 3h40m**,
against hardware that was not there at all.

Two independent things say that is the wrong shape:

- **The information was already free.** `AudioDiagnostics` reads
  `kAudioHardwarePropertyDevices` and the per-device properties every five
  seconds, entirely with `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` property queries that open
  nothing. The expensive question was never buying an answer we didn't have.
- **The symptom shape is a known CoreAudio failure with this exact fingerprint.**
  `AVAudioEngine`'s hidden aggregate going stale presents as *engine running,
  buffers completing, no audio* — which is our no-signal state precisely, and it
  is documented on the output side with "only switching the device and back fixes
  it" (our replug). Ours had gone further than a stale aggregate, since `killall
  coreaudiod` did not clear it — but the failure family is the same, and we were
  churning the exact object at the centre of it.

So `finishListening()` now calls `requireSettledInputDevice()` **before**
`prepareFormat()`, and it throws into the existing failed-start catch — so a
refusal reuses the whole logged/counted/retried path rather than growing a second
recovery mechanism beside it. Two requirements:

- **A device the HAL says is openable**, judged by `AudioDiagnostics.hasUsableInput`:
  non-aggregate (counting our own aggregate would report a usable input *because*
  we already opened one), alive, and with a **nonzero rate and sane channel
  count** — mere presence is the `outputFormat` trap one layer down.
- **Continuously present for `deviceSettleDelay` (6s)**, which is longer than the
  5s sample interval, so the gate can never be satisfied by the same observation
  that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened the mic *in the same
  second it appeared* — via the config-change handler, not the ladder, which is
  why the gate belongs at `finishListening` where both paths meet.

Effect on the measured outage: **~210 device opens → 0.** Nothing is opened until
there is something to open.

**What is proven and what is not.** Proven: the churn was real, was
under-costed by its own comment, and is unlike any ordinary audio app. *Not*
proven: that it caused the wedge. The mic reported a sane `48000Hz/2ch/alive=y`
when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the mid-enumeration story
specifically. Treat this as removing the only mechanism by which we could
plausibly damage a device — not as a confirmed root-cause fix. **If it recurs,
that is information, not a reason to assume the gate failed.**

Stop building an AVAudioEngine to ask whether a microphone exists (#88)

No other app on this Mac wedges the mic on sleep, so the previous
conclusion — "the wedge survives coreaudiod, therefore nothing in our
process can be responsible" — was wrong. "Irreversible once triggered"
and "not caused by us" are separate claims, and only the first was
established.

Reading AudioHub rather than its summary: prepareFormat() ->
renewEngine() -> makeEngine(), and makeEngine() touches
engine.inputNode. That property access opens the default input device
and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod
(CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>); a failed start tears it back
down. So a "retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus
an aggregate create/destroy, and the measured outage ran that cycle
~210 times over 3h40m against hardware that was not there at all. The
ladder's own comment claimed it was "a cheap format read"; the
lifecycle doc had already recorded that this was false, and nothing
acted on it.

The information was free the whole time. AudioDiagnostics reads the
HAL every five seconds with AudioObjectGetPropertyData property
queries that open nothing, so the expensive question was never buying
an answer we didn't already have.

- AudioDiagnostics exposes usableInputFor: how long CoreAudio has
  continuously offered an input we could actually open. hasUsableInput
  excludes aggregates (counting our own would report a usable input
  *because* we already opened one) and requires a nonzero rate and sane
  channel count, not mere presence — the outputFormat trap one layer
  down.
- finishListening() calls requireSettledInputDevice() before
  prepareFormat(), throwing into the existing failed-start catch so a
  refusal reuses the logged/counted/retried path instead of growing a
  second recovery mechanism beside it.
- The gate also requires the device to have been present for 6s, longer
  than the 5s sample interval, so it can never be satisfied by the same
  observation that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened
  the mic in the same second it appeared — via the config-change
  handler, not the ladder, which is why the gate sits at
  finishListening where both paths meet.

Effect on the measured outage: ~210 device opens -> 0.

Not claimed as a confirmed root-cause fix. The mic reported a sane
48000Hz/2ch/alive=y when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the
mid-enumeration story specifically. This removes the only mechanism by
which we could plausibly damage a device; whether it was the mechanism
is still open, and the doc says so.

the no-signal wedge honestly instead of claiming to listen (#88)

The wedge recurred on 0.4.1 and was measured end to end for the first
time. It arrived in a shape neither open theory predicted: no AUDIO
STALL at all. Buffers arrived at the full rate (3545 per 600s against a
theoretical 3515) from a device reporting alive=y/running=y/48000Hz/2ch,
with every sample exactly zero, for half an hour, system-wide.

The escalation ladder is the finding. Quitting the app (full
applicationWillTerminate teardown) did not clear it; `killall
coreaudiod` did not clear it; physically re-plugging the mic did. So
this wedge lives below coreaudiod, in the device/USB layer — it
survives every client dying and the audio daemon restarting. No
in-process recovery can work, and a restart ladder against it would be
pure churn against a state it cannot fix.

So the fix is reporting, not recovery. `no signal` was already being
detected and logged at ERROR every ten minutes, and it drove nothing:
isStalled tripped only on *absent* buffers, so the menu bar showed 😄
"listening" for the whole outage while the log said the opposite —
the sin #79 set out to kill, recurring one layer up.

- AudioDiagnostics publishes a three-state `health` (ok / stalled /
  noSignal) in place of the isStalled bool, with one setHealth() that
  logs the transition and notifies, so the log and the menu bar cannot
  disagree.
- No-signal is judged on the 5s sample tick over a 60s run of all-zero
  buffers, not inside the 600s heartbeat block — caught in a minute
  rather than ten, and logged once per transition rather than repeating
  an identical ERROR every ten minutes for as long as it lasts.
- The icon (⚠️), status line, tooltip and menu tooltip all render the
  new state, and the no-signal remedy names the *only* thing measured
  to work: unplug and reconnect. It explicitly does not offer "Restart
  listening", which is measured not to help.

Detection thresholds are unchanged for the stall path. 60s of exact
zeros cannot be a quiet room: a real capsule always has a noise floor
and the window covers ~350 buffers.

dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md records the escalation ladder,
marks the superseded "wait for an AUDIO STALL with running=y"
instruction, and keeps the one unsettled suspect: we opened the device
in the same second it reappeared.

building an AVAudioEngine to ask whether a microphone exists (#88)

No other app on this Mac wedges the mic on sleep, so the previous
conclusion — "the wedge survives coreaudiod, therefore nothing in our
process can be responsible" — was wrong. "Irreversible once triggered"
and "not caused by us" are separate claims, and only the first was
established.

Reading AudioHub rather than its summary: prepareFormat() ->
renewEngine() -> makeEngine(), and makeEngine() touches
engine.inputNode. That property access opens the default input device
and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod
(CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>); a failed start tears it back
down. So a "retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus
an aggregate create/destroy, and the measured outage ran that cycle
~210 times over 3h40m against hardware that was not there at all. The
ladder's own comment claimed it was "a cheap format read"; the
lifecycle doc had already recorded that this was false, and nothing
acted on it.

The information was free the whole time. AudioDiagnostics reads the
HAL every five seconds with AudioObjectGetPropertyData property
queries that open nothing, so the expensive question was never buying
an answer we didn't already have.

- AudioDiagnostics exposes usableInputFor: how long CoreAudio has
  continuously offered an input we could actually open. hasUsableInput
  excludes aggregates (counting our own would report a usable input
  *because* we already opened one) and requires a nonzero rate and sane
  channel count, not mere presence — the outputFormat trap one layer
  down.
- finishListening() calls requireSettledInputDevice() before
  prepareFormat(), throwing into the existing failed-start catch so a
  refusal reuses the logged/counted/retried path instead of growing a
  second recovery mechanism beside it.
- The gate also requires the device to have been present for 6s, longer
  than the 5s sample interval, so it can never be satisfied by the same
  observation that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened
  the mic in the same second it appeared — via the config-change
  handler, not the ladder, which is why the gate sits at
  finishListening where both paths meet.

Effect on the measured outage: ~210 device opens -> 0.

Not claimed as a confirmed root-cause fix. The mic reported a sane
48000Hz/2ch/alive=y when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the
mid-enumeration story specifically. This removes the only mechanism by
which we could plausibly damage a device; whether it was the mechanism
is still open, and the doc says so.

the no-signal wedge honestly instead of claiming to listen (#88)

The wedge recurred on 0.4.1 and was measured end to end for the first
time. It arrived in a shape neither open theory predicted: no AUDIO
STALL at all. Buffers arrived at the full rate (3545 per 600s against a
theoretical 3515) from a device reporting alive=y/running=y/48000Hz/2ch,
with every sample exactly zero, for half an hour, system-wide.

The escalation ladder is the finding. Quitting the app (full
applicationWillTerminate teardown) did not clear it; `killall
coreaudiod` did not clear it; physically re-plugging the mic did. So
this wedge lives below coreaudiod, in the device/USB layer — it
survives every client dying and the audio daemon restarting. No
in-process recovery can work, and a restart ladder against it would be
pure churn against a state it cannot fix.

So the fix is reporting, not recovery. `no signal` was already being
detected and logged at ERROR every ten minutes, and it drove nothing:
isStalled tripped only on *absent* buffers, so the menu bar showed 😄
"listening" for the whole outage while the log said the opposite —
the sin #79 set out to kill, recurring one layer up.

- AudioDiagnostics publishes a three-state `health` (ok / stalled /
  noSignal) in place of the isStalled bool, with one setHealth() that
  logs the transition and notifies, so the log and the menu bar cannot
  disagree.
- No-signal is judged on the 5s sample tick over a 60s run of all-zero
  buffers, not inside the 600s heartbeat block — caught in a minute
  rather than ten, and logged once per transition rather than repeating
  an identical ERROR every ten minutes for as long as it lasts.
- The icon (⚠️), status line, tooltip and menu tooltip all render the
  new state, and the no-signal remedy names the *only* thing measured
  to work: unplug and reconnect. It explicitly does not offer "Restart
  listening", which is measured not to help.

Detection thresholds are unchanged for the stall path. 60s of exact
zeros cannot be a quiet room: a real capsule always has a noise floor
and the window covers ~350 buffers.

dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md records the escalation ladder,
marks the superseded "wait for an AUDIO STALL with running=y"
instruction, and keeps the one unsettled suspect: we opened the device
in the same second it reappeared.

content.text: Run 42 (the reporting commit) **compiled and built the DMG successfully on macOS** — so that half is verified past the compiler. Run 43 (this change) is in progress. Updating the PR to match its new scope:

input.title: Stop churning the input device, and report the no-signal wedge honestly (#88)
input.body:
Fixes the reporting failure in #88, and removes the app behaviour that most plausibly caused it.

## What was measured

The wedge recurred on 0.4.1 and was captured live. There was **no `AUDIO STALL`** — buffers arrived at the full rate (3545 per 600s vs a theoretical 3515) from a device reporting `alive=y/running=y/48000Hz/2ch`, with **every sample exactly zero**, for half an hour, system-wide.

```
05:01:18  could not start listening: … inputs=NONE     ← 3h40m of this, once a minute
05:01:45  displays woke while listening was down
05:01:48  WARN  input devices changed — *"Logitech BRIO"/usb/48000Hz/2ch/alive=y
05:01:48  audio configuration changed — reconfiguring
05:01:48  listening started (sampleRate=48000, channels=2)   ← same second
05:12:33  ERROR  no signal: 3545 buffers … every sample was zero
```

Owner-run escalation ladder, in order: quitting LaughCounter (full teardown) — **no**; `sudo killall coreaudiod` — **no**; physically re-plugging the mic — **yes**.

## Correcting a wrong conclusion

The first pass read that ladder as "the wedge survives coreaudiod, therefore nothing in our process can be responsible." That conflates two separate claims. It establishes the state is *irreversible once triggered*; it says nothing about **what triggers it**. And no other app on this Mac wedges the mic on sleep — so something we do is abnormal.

## The abnormal thing

`AudioHub.prepareFormat()` → `renewEngine()` → `makeEngine()`, and `makeEngine()` touches `engine.inputNode`. **That property access opens the default input device and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod** (`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>`); a failed start tears it back down.

So a "retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus an aggregate create/destroy, run **~210 times over 3h40m** against hardware that was not there at all. The ladder's own comment claimed it was "a cheap format read"; `dev/procedures/mac-audio-lifecycle.md` had already recorded that this was false, and nothing acted on it.

Two things say this is the wrong shape:

- **The information was free the whole time.** `AudioDiagnostics` already reads `kAudioHardwarePropertyDevices` and per-device properties every 5s using `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` — property queries that open nothing. The expensive question was never buying an answer we didn't have.
- **The symptom shape is a documented CoreAudio failure with this exact fingerprint.** `AVAudioEngine`'s hidden aggregate going stale presents as *engine running, buffers completing, no audio* — our no-signal state precisely, documented on the output side with "only switching the device and back fixes it" (our replug). Ours had gone further, since `killall coreaudiod` didn't clear it — but we were churning the exact object at the centre of that failure family. ([cc-skills#73](https://github.com/terrylica/cc-skills/issues/73))

## Changes

**1. Never build an engine to ask whether a mic exists.** `finishListening()` calls `requireSettledInputDevice()` **before** `prepareFormat()`, throwing into the existing failed-start catch so a refusal reuses the logged/counted/retried path rather than growing a second recovery mechanism beside it. It requires:

- a device the HAL says is openable — `hasUsableInput` excludes aggregates (counting our own would report a usable input *because* we already opened one) and demands a **nonzero rate and sane channel count**, not mere presence, which is the `outputFormat` trap one layer down;
- continuous presence for `deviceSettleDelay` (6s) — longer than the 5s sample interval, so the gate can never be satisfied by the same observation that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened the mic *in the same second it appeared*, via the config-change handler rather than the ladder, which is why the gate sits at `finishListening()` where both paths meet.

**Effect on the measured outage: ~210 device opens → 0.**

**2. Report the failure honestly.** `no signal` was already detected and logged at ERROR every ten minutes and drove **nothing** — `isStalled` tripped only on *absent* buffers, so the menu bar showed 😄 "listening" for the whole outage while the log said the opposite. That's the sin #79 set out to kill, recurring one layer up.

- `AudioDiagnostics` publishes three-state `health` (`ok`/`stalled`/`noSignal`) via a single `setHealth()` that logs the transition and notifies, so log and menu bar cannot disagree.
- No-signal judged on the 5s tick over a 60s zero-run, not inside the 600s heartbeat: caught in a minute rather than ten, logged once per transition instead of repeating forever.
- Icon (⚠️), status line and both tooltips render it, and the remedy names the only thing measured to work — unplug and reconnect. It deliberately does not offer "Restart listening".

## What is and isn't claimed

**Proven:** the churn was real, was under-costed by its own comment, and is unlike any ordinary audio app.

**Not proven:** that it caused the wedge. The mic reported a sane `48000Hz/2ch/alive=y` when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the mid-enumeration story specifically. This removes the only mechanism by which we could plausibly damage a device — it is not a confirmed root-cause fix, and the doc says so. If it recurs, that is information, not proof the gate failed.

## Verification

`swift build` can't run in a Linux session; the branch DMG workflow compiles it on macOS. Per the lifecycle doc, **compile-green was never a gate for this file** — two crash-on-launch builds have shipped past CI before, so this isn't verified until it has started on a Mac.

Live check on a healthy launch: still 😄, and `audio health: listening … peak=<nonzero>`. The gate is visible as a one-retry delay before `listening started` after a device appears.

building an AVAudioEngine to ask whether a microphone exists (#88)

No other app on this Mac wedges the mic on sleep, so the previous
conclusion — "the wedge survives coreaudiod, therefore nothing in our
process can be responsible" — was wrong. "Irreversible once triggered"
and "not caused by us" are separate claims, and only the first was
established.

Reading AudioHub rather than its summary: prepareFormat() ->
renewEngine() -> makeEngine(), and makeEngine() touches
engine.inputNode. That property access opens the default input device
and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod
(CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>); a failed start tears it back
down. So a "retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus
an aggregate create/destroy, and the measured outage ran that cycle
~210 times over 3h40m against hardware that was not there at all. The
ladder's own comment claimed it was "a cheap format read"; the
lifecycle doc had already recorded that this was false, and nothing
acted on it.

The information was free the whole time. AudioDiagnostics reads the
HAL every five seconds with AudioObjectGetPropertyData property
queries that open nothing, so the expensive question was never buying
an answer we didn't already have.

- AudioDiagnostics exposes usableInputFor: how long CoreAudio has
  continuously offered an input we could actually open. hasUsableInput
  excludes aggregates (counting our own would report a usable input
  *because* we already opened one) and requires a nonzero rate and sane
  channel count, not mere presence — the outputFormat trap one layer
  down.
- finishListening() calls requireSettledInputDevice() before
  prepareFormat(), throwing into the existing failed-start catch so a
  refusal reuses the logged/counted/retried path instead of growing a
  second recovery mechanism beside it.
- The gate also requires the device to have been present for 6s, longer
  than the 5s sample interval, so it can never be satisfied by the same
  observation that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened
  the mic in the same second it appeared — via the config-change
  handler, not the ladder, which is why the gate sits at
  finishListening where both paths meet.

Effect on the measured outage: ~210 device opens -> 0.

Not claimed as a confirmed root-cause fix. The mic reported a sane
48000Hz/2ch/alive=y when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the
mid-enumeration story specifically. This removes the only mechanism by
which we could plausibly damage a device; whether it was the mechanism
is still open, and the doc says so.

lastPrompt: Have you done some resaerch on what is going on? This is a bug of our doing. No other app renders the microphone unusable when the computer sleeps.

content.text:
Comment class: correction — my earlier conclusion was wrong, and this replaces it.

**CI green on both commits.** ([run 43](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/actions/runs/30664419981) — DMG built, so the whole change compiles on macOS.)

You were right on both counts. I hadn't researched, and I'd drawn a conclusion the evidence didn't support: "the wedge survives coreaudiod, therefore nothing in our process caused it." That conflates *irreversible once triggered* with *not caused by us*. Your ladder established the first. It says nothing about the second — and "no other app does this" is the argument I should have taken seriously.

## What the research turned up

**The symptom shape is a documented CoreAudio failure, not exotic.** `AVAudioEngine` mints a hidden per-client aggregate device (`CADefaultDeviceAggregate-*`) at init, and it can go stale: engine running, buffers completing, no audio. That is our state exactly, documented on the output side with "only switching the device and back fixes it" — our replug. ([cc-skills#73](https://github.com/terrylica/cc-skills/issues/73))

**And we were churning that exact object, at a rate nothing else does.** Reading `AudioHub` instead of its summary: `makeEngine()` touches `engine.inputNode`, and *that property access* opens the default input and mints the aggregate. So every retry was a device open plus an aggregate create/destroy — **~210 of them across your 3h40m outage**, against hardware that wasn't there at all.

The ladder's own comment called this "a cheap format read." Your lifecycle doc had already recorded that this was false. Nothing had acted on it.

**And the answer was free the whole time.** `AudioDiagnostics` already reads the HAL every 5 seconds with `AudioObjectGetPropertyData` — property queries that open nothing. We were paying a device open to learn something we already knew.

## What I changed

`finishListening()` — where both the retry ladder *and* the config-change handler converge — now calls `requireSettledInputDevice()` **before** `prepareFormat()`. It demands a non-aggregate device that's alive with a nonzero rate (mere presence is the `outputFormat` trap one layer down), continuously present for 6s — longer than the sample interval, so it can never be satisfied by the same observation that first revealed the device. That was the same-second grab, and it came through the config-change handler, not the ladder.

It throws into the existing failed-start catch, so a refusal reuses the whole logged/counted/retried path rather than growing a second mechanism beside it.

**~210 device opens per outage → 0.**

Plus the reporting fix from before: three-state `health`, ⚠️ in the menu bar, detection in 60s instead of 600s, and a remedy line that says *unplug it* rather than *restart listening*.

## Two things you should know before merging

**A real tradeoff:** recovery after the mic returns is now ~6s slower, because we wait for it to settle instead of grabbing it instantly.

**Still not a proven root-cause fix.** The BRIO reported a sane `48000Hz/2ch/alive=y` when we grabbed it — which argues *against* the mid-enumeration story specifically. What this does is remove the only mechanism by which we could plausibly damage a device. If it recurs, that's information, not proof the gate failed. The doc says so explicitly, so a future session doesn't mistake this for settled.

> ⚠️ Still open: PR #100 is green and ready for review. The DMG artifact is on [run 43](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/actions/runs/30664419981) if you want to install it and let the next display sleep exercise it — that's the only real test. Say "bump version" if you'd like 0.4.2 rather than refreshing the 0.4.1 Release.

creates/updates the GitHub Release for the app's current version (read from
`Info.plist`), attaching `LaughCounter.dmg` — which is what the
[latest-release download link](https://github.com/missingbulb/LaughCounter/releases/latest/download/LaughCounter.dmg)
resolves to.

So to **ship a new version**, bump `CFBundleShortVersionString` in
`Resources/Info.plist` and merge to `main` — a new `v<version>` Release appears on
its own. (Merges that keep the same version just refresh that Release's DMG.) You
can also publish a Release from the GitHub UI, or run the workflow manually from
the Actions tab.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later in the repo's scheduled `conversation-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.

building an AVAudioEngine to ask whether a microphone exists (#88)

No other app on this Mac wedges the mic on sleep, so the previous
conclusion — "the wedge survives coreaudiod, therefore nothing in our
process can be responsible" — was wrong. "Irreversible once triggered"
and "not caused by us" are separate claims, and only the first was
established.

Reading AudioHub rather than its summary: prepareFormat() ->
renewEngine() -> makeEngine(), and makeEngine() touches
engine.inputNode. That property access opens the default input device
and mints a hidden per-client aggregate device inside coreaudiod
(CADefaultDeviceAggregate-<pid>-<n>); a failed start tears it back
down. So a "retry" was never a format read — it was a device open plus
an aggregate create/destroy, and the measured outage ran that cycle
~210 times over 3h40m against hardware that was not there at all. The
ladder's own comment claimed it was "a cheap format read"; the
lifecycle doc had already recorded that this was false, and nothing
acted on it.

The information was free the whole time. AudioDiagnostics reads the
HAL every five seconds with AudioObjectGetPropertyData property
queries that open nothing, so the expensive question was never buying
an answer we didn't already have.

- AudioDiagnostics exposes usableInputFor: how long CoreAudio has
  continuously offered an input we could actually open. hasUsableInput
  excludes aggregates (counting our own would report a usable input
  *because* we already opened one) and requires a nonzero rate and sane
  channel count, not mere presence — the outputFormat trap one layer
  down.
- finishListening() calls requireSettledInputDevice() before
  prepareFormat(), throwing into the existing failed-start catch so a
  refusal reuses the logged/counted/retried path instead of growing a
  second recovery mechanism beside it.
- The gate also requires the device to have been present for 6s, longer
  than the 5s sample interval, so it can never be satisfied by the same
  observation that first revealed the device. The wedge episode opened
  the mic in the same second it appeared — via the config-change
  handler, not the ladder, which is why the gate sits at
  finishListening where both paths meet.

Effect on the measured outage: ~210 device opens -> 0.

Not claimed as a confirmed root-cause fix. The mic reported a sane
48000Hz/2ch/alive=y when we grabbed it, which is evidence against the
mid-enumeration story specifically. This removes the only mechanism by
which we could plausibly damage a device; whether it was the mechanism
is still open, and the doc says so.
